html:
Pasion's bank was the largest bank in Athens in the early 4th century BCE. Its owner, Pasion, began life as a slave and became one of the richest men in the city and an Athenian citizen.

Pasion worked for two bankers in Piraeus, the port of Athens. They freed him, and he took over the business. Athenian bankers sat at tables in the market, changing the many kinds of Greek coin, such as the Athenian owl, keeping deposits and making loans, often to merchants shipping grain and other goods across the sea. Pasion also owned a shield factory. He gave the city a thousand shields and paid for warships, and in return the Assembly granted him citizenship, an honour very rarely given.

When he died around 370 BCE, he left the bank to his own former slave, Phormion, who married his widow. Pasion's son Apollodorus later sued Phormion over the inheritance. Speeches from these lawsuits survive among the works of Demosthenes and are among our best sources on Greek banking and on how slaves, freedmen and citizens mixed in the business world of Athens.
sum: Pasion's bank was the largest bank in Athens in the early 4th century BCE. Its owner, Pasion, began life as a slave and became one of the richest men in the city and an Athenian citizen.
